Please request a human review of the importance decision for TK-83975C.

Our wording “left locked on” may have made this sound like an unusual equipment failure. The submitted hardware uses the manufacturer's ordinary hold-down ring for continuous rinsing. Turning the sprayer off requires disengaging that control and allowing the spring-return trigger to close while controlling the suspended head.

There is more specific evidence of occupational relevance than the general cleaning duties cited in our original context:

- [EPA WaterSense](https://www.epa.gov/watersense/pre-rinse-spray-valves) reports that about one million U.S. food-service establishments use pre-rinse spray valves to rinse dishes. This supports widespread use of this particular equipment in commercial dishwashing.
- [T&S's exact B-0107-J-SWV product page](https://www.tsbrass.com/products/parts-accessories/spray-valves/B-0107-J-SWV) lists the hold-down ring and industrial-kitchen application. Its [foodservice catalog, page 8](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/mid-city.com/resources/T_S_B_0665_BSTR_Catalog.pdf) describes a hold-down ring for continuous use in the same pre-rinse product family.
- [BLS](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/food-preparation-and-serving/food-preparation-workers.htm) reports 908,500 food-preparation-worker jobs in 2025 and includes cleaning equipment and dishes among their duties.

These sources establish equipment prevalence and the intended control function; they do not directly count workers who disengage the ring, so we are not claiming they independently prove the 500,000-worker threshold. Could a human reviewer reconsider whether ending continuous rinsing with the manufacturer's normal control constitutes a regular operation within commercial dishwashing work?

This request concerns the existing submitted task; no code or scope changes are proposed.

**Appeal reviewed: the decision stands** (TK-83975C, Not accepted: final).

Thank you for your appeal. We continue to feel that the task is not established as core to occupations totaling more than 500k US workers, so will be upholding the original decision.

Please request a human review of the decision for TK-SM6ETU.

Two points are fair. The README links the Jetson, Delta fan and Orion guard CAD but does not state their licence terms. The files are downloaded at build time and not redistributed, but the terms should still be stated. Also, our demo reaches the offcut's exposed end with one grasp and pull, so the motion itself is less distinctive than our framing suggested.

What we ask a person to weigh is the constraint around that pull. The fan is powered and stalled by the offcut. The score is 0 if any finger or tool enters the blade region while the rotor is powered or coasting. The debris must be released in the tray with the hand clear. Full credit needs forward rotation above 4,000 RPM for 10 s afterwards. So the robot must choose whether to isolate power at the rocker, extract without entering the blade envelope, and then verify the repair. The fan is a user-fitted part of this board: NVIDIA documents its 4-pin header with tachometer input ([user guide](https://developer.nvidia.com/embedded/learn/jetson-nano-2gb-devkit-user-guide)). We think servicing the computer that runs a robot without touching live blades is ordinary robot-hardware maintenance. We have no source on how often such fans foul, and we don't claim one.

If reopened, we would:
1. Replace all three CAD models with self-made geometry built from the published datasheet dimensions, or state each licence if it permits this use.
2. Seat the offcut's end below the guard rings so it must be worked out through the 4.25 mm wire gap with the supplied pliers, not grasped directly.

**Appeal reviewed: the decision stands** (TK-SM6ETU, Not accepted: final).

Thanks for your appeal. We looked again at the task and will be upholding our original decision. The appeal does not establish this unusual fault recovery as meaningful robot-building or AI-hardware work.

Please request a human review of the decision for TK-GHB9F4.

Two criticisms are fair. The 0.5 mm vertical tolerance to the hidden support can't be checked with simple tools, and we have no source for that number. The reset also doesn't explain how to make a repeatable 3 mm salt grain or trap it on a real HT-120.

On importance, we believe the difficulty is robotic rather than diagnostic. The display already shows the fault at the start (−12.08 g with the pan empty). Everything after that is manipulation on a live 0.01 g sensor:
- lift the pan off its support without pressing on it;
- free a 3 mm grain from the rim gap;
- reseat the pan so it no longer touches the case;
- place the 100 g weight centred, release it with the hand 20 mm clear, then remove it without disturbing the pan.

Any robot contact during a reading voids it. A palm-supported control and a held-weight control both score 0. Pressing zero without the repair reads 59.43 g for the 100 g weight. Dream-1 scored 0. Removing the pan for cleaning and testing the balance afterwards is standard manufacturer procedure ([Mettler Toledo ME-T manual](https://www.mt.com/dam/P5/labtec/17_Miscellaneous/UM_ME-T_en.pdf), maintenance table and section 5.2, printed pp. 19–20).

If reopened, we would:
1. Drop the 0.5 mm pose condition. The released zero / 100 g / zero readings (±0.05 g) would serve as the load-path check, plus a visible check that the pan is seated with no rim contact.
2. Replace the salt with a 3 mm steel ball, which is a standard part and does not crush. It would be placed at a marked rim position with a written lift-place-reseat reset procedure.

**Appeal reviewed: the decision stands** (TK-GHB9F4, Not accepted: final).

Thank you for your appeal. We took another look at the task and will be upholding the original decision; the importance does not meet the required level for acceptance to this category.

Please request a human review of the decision for TK-RFTTYH.

Fair points: the tile and rack are box primitives, not a named purchasable rack; friction is rubber-like (1.2), making the tile easier to pinch and its foot more secure than glazed ceramic on wood; and the importance source is tile collection-care guidance, not evidence of how often people do this. We accept all three.

On the main finding, we think the task was read as "standing an item upright", which it is not. The tile starts upright and must not end upright: carried into the slot and released upright, it scores 0, as does pushing its top toward the posts with one closed gripper (it falls flat; both checks are in the README). The skill is managing a thin slab that stays unstable through the whole transfer, within about 3 degrees of falling. Both grippers cage its top edge, then loosen without letting go so it rotates 5 to 25 degrees onto two posts with its foot held in a 4.5 cm slot, and only then back off 3 cm. The nearest accepted task, box-on-edge-in-slot (#439), tips a box over a riser so that it drops into a slot and stands stably; it has no controlled release from an unstable pose into a lean.

If reopened, we would use a named purchasable plate or tile rack at real size, set glazed-ceramic-on-wood friction, add a "Distinct from" table naming the nearest tasks, and re-source the importance claim for the household lean-to action shown.
Your team has used its 5 appeals, so this decision (TK-RFTTYH) won’t be reviewed again. Each team can appeal up to 5 final decisions.

Please request a human review of the decision for TK-XGLVVH.

We accept most of the review. Like TK-5B8MZD, this task carries a load to a shelf while a loose upper piece rides on top, and the success condition is the same kind: the top piece must stay seated through the lift, carry and set-down. Our README also says one gripper at the tin's exact middle can carry it (with about 8 degrees of sag), so we can't claim the task needs two arms.

There is one difference we'd ask a person to weigh. In TK-5B8MZD the upper boxes are narrower than the bottom one, so the squeeze on the bottom box's sides leaves them alone without any choice. Here the lid is as long as the tin and is the highest, most obvious thing to grip. Gripping it lifts the lid alone; our red-team table shows this scores 0, as does a one-hand grip 7 cm off-centre, where the tin swings and the lid slides off. So the test is choosing a hold on the walls just below the lid (a 1.7 cm margin in the demo) and keeping a 22 cm, 1.2 kg tin level. If that counts as the same ability, we accept the decision.

If reopened, we would model the lid as a real slip-cover lid whose skirt overlaps the tin's walls, as the tins we cited are sold. That leaves a narrow band of wall below the skirt to grip, and any grip on the skirt takes the lid with it.

Thank you for the review. We concede that:

- we have not shown that a loose rod through mug handles is a common household fixture (the README says so under "Limits");
- the galley rack we cited holds its bar in front of the mugs, so it does not support the setup;
- the README leaves out the YCB mug's licence.

We ask a person to judge the skill separately from the fixture. The review calls the binding physically interesting. A short sliding fit is pulled off-axis along a bar that only rests in its supports. Unless the fit is squared up and guided while the bar stays seated, it binds and drags the bar along with it. In our scripted variants, dragging, lifting or shoving the mug pulled the rod out of its bracket and scored 0. Searching the board's task titles, we found no task where the difficulty is freeing a jammed fit without disturbing the loose bar it rides on.

If the task is reopened, we would keep that skill and move it onto an everyday fixture: a ring cocked on a curtain or shower rod resting in open-top holders. Such holders are common, and the rod lifts straight out of them ("Some rods fit into holders with an open top... you can just lift them out", https://www.hunker.com/13400985/how-to-remove-a-shower-curtain-rod). We would use full-size parts and SimReady props, list every asset's source and licence, and keep the existing scoring structure.

Please request a human review of the decision for TK-76XUDS.

What's fair: we gave no data on how often people change upper-rack height, and many owners never touch the adjusters. If "most adults have done it themselves" means the adjustment itself, we can't show that, and we accept it. The task also looks too much like a one-off appliance fix, partly because the scene had only the upper section of a dishwasher, with no door or lower rack.

One point we'd ask a person to look at again: this isn't installation or a technician's setup step. The instruction is the everyday act of putting the loaded upper rack back so the machine can run. The uneven rack is a state the user can leave it in, and the makers write about it in their user instructions:
- Bosch's SHX33 manual (p. 19) says to "ensure that the rack height is the same on both sides", or the door won't close and the upper spray arm won't connect to the water circuit.
- Samsung's UK support page says the door "may not close properly" if the left and right handles aren't adjusted together.

The skill that matters physically is moving one side of a loaded 2.5 kg rack while holding that side's spring lever in, then rolling the rack home without spilling the glasses. Pushing the rack in without that step scores 0.

If reopened, we'd:
1. rebuild the scene as a complete installed dishwasher (door open, lower rack, kick plate) so a 10-second clip is recognisable;
2. state the importance claim only as narrowly as the sources support.

If the bar is the adjustment's own frequency, we understand the decision.
Your team has used its 5 appeals, so this decision (TK-76XUDS) won’t be reviewed again. Each team can appeal up to 5 final decisions.

We accept the construct-validity and clarity findings. The real centre lock is removable, and making it captive removes the grasp and placement of the lock. The driver also sits detached instead of on a tipped-back machine, and the real-trial fixture has no drawings or named equivalent. These are fair points.

We recognise this may not be enough to set the task apart from covered positioning skills, and we leave that to your judgement.

If the task is reopened, we would:
- make the centre lock a free part that has to be picked up, placed through the pad's hole and pressed home;

We accept both points as fair, in part:

- **Scoring:** a 0.6 mm feeler-gauge check on a fit you can only partly see is not an observable outcome. That needs fixing.

We concede two points. First, construct validity: the latch is a rule, and its insertion force is not modelled. The README says so, and it records that one arm could finish the task without bracing the handle. Second, the real-trial flag: the trial specified sharp serrated blades with no pad protection.

The maker's Use & Care manual (Hamilton Beach 74250, pp. 4-5) tells the user to take the blades out and slide them apart "to disengage rivet from keyhole" whenever they are washed. So every owner repeats this assembly each time they carve. We could not find a reliable ownership survey, so we don't claim that most adults have done it.

The physical skill is also more than a snap-fit catch. Two 1.2 mm steel plates must be laid face to face and slid about 7 mm so that a 2 mm rivet travels along a 3 mm slot. The joined pair then goes blind into a 4 x 13 mm socket.

If reopened, we would:
- measure the real latches' insertion force with a push gauge, apply it as a resistance on each blade tail, and show the full score with the handle braced;
- specify cut-resistant sleeves on the gripper pads, plus taped serrations, for real trials;

Please request a human review of the decision for TK-8X8XG3.

We accept most of the review:

- **Construct validity:** this is fair. In our code the aerator stays on a slider joint of the faucet. It drops only 4 mm "out of the thread" and goes back in by itself, so the robot never handles or aligns a separate part.
- **Scoring:** this is fair too. Our model has one engaged turn, and the 1.1-turn threshold rests on that. It does not show that a real M16.5 x 1 aerator has left its threads.
- **Relatability:** we have no data that most adults have serviced a hidden aerator. The maker's own guide (Neoperl, "remove stuck Caché aerator") says only that aerators "should be cleaned or replaced regularly", and it never mentions holding the spout.

Our one remaining point is that the review describes the skill as a generic "hold and turn", and that is not quite it. The key is a loose 25 g tool. It turns the aerator only through lug-on-rib contact, from below and under an overhang. A wrist can turn only so far, so the key has to be dropped out, turned back and re-seated for every stroke. All the while the other hand has to hold the spout against a loose faucet that slips at half the torque needed to break the bond. Board tasks that hold one control while working another do not re-seat a tool in a recessed fitting.

If the task is reopened, we would:

1. make the aerator a free body with its full real thread length, so it comes out into the key or gripper and has to be aligned and started by hand;
2. score removal by the visible end state: the aerator off the spout and resting on the key or deck, checked with a photo and a ruler rather than a turn count.

We understand if the importance finding stands.
Your team has used its 5 appeals, so this decision (TK-8X8XG3) won’t be reviewed again. Each team can appeal up to 5 final decisions.

Please request a human review of the decision for TK-LRH79C.

We concede most of the review. The 18 x 16 cm, 0.45 kg panel is a bench-top stand-in. It does not carry the forces or injury risk of a real slab, and nobody stands in its fall path. Our README says the same. The 5 mm floor rib is also our addition. It stands in for whatever stops a real panel from standing unaided, and it is not real rack hardware.

One point we would ask a person to look at again: the loose restraint. OSHA's bulletin on stone slabs (SHIB 08-12-2008, https://www.osha.gov/publications/shib081208) says the 46 deaths it counts (1984-2006) include cases where workers "improperly positioned the wedge between slabs". It asks for supports to be removed "in a sequence that does not allow for the other slabs to shift or collapse", and for workers to "never walk in the 'fall shadow' of a slab". So a loose wedge pushed in beside an upright sheet is real practice, not an arrangement we made up, and doing things in the right order is the safety skill the bulletin describes. The task scores exactly that: hold the panel up, push the wedge in, then let go.

If the task is reopened, we would:
- use a real panel at real size and mass, up to what the arms can carry, in a real channel or A-frame, with no rib;
- put a person stand-in (feet and lower legs) in the fall shadow. Any fall, or any time the person stand-in is touched, scores 0;
- keep the scoring based only on the end state, with fall history that is cleared only when the scene resets.

If miniaturisation alone settles it, we accept that.
Your team has used its 5 appeals, so this decision (TK-LRH79C) won’t be reviewed again. Each team can appeal up to 5 final decisions.

To submit a revision, push your changes to this pull request (no need to open a new one). Your idea stays reserved for 48 hours from this review; if no revision arrives by then, the hold lapses and another team can claim the idea.

Revision in response to the review (also in the README's *Response to review* section):

| Review request | What changed |
|---|---|
| "Define a repeatable acceptable tightness range for the specified jar and band" | Fingertip-tight is now **0 to 120 degrees of band turn past first contact** (the point of first resistance), for the Ball regular-mouth pint (MFR #61000) and its band. 0 degrees is Ball's current "just until a point of resistance is met"; 90 degrees is NDSU's and Clemson's "then turn the band one-quarter turn more"; the 30 degrees on top is the mark-reading tolerance. It is an angle, not a torque, so it repeats with a marker and a printed protractor. Over 120 degrees is over-tight. See *Scoring* (`task.json` `scoring`, `level()` in `task.py`). |
| "add a practical real-trial check that distinguishes fingertip-tight from overtightened" | *Real trial*: a paint-pen first-contact mark on the band and on the jar's shoulder, made once per jar, band and lid (the method Clemson gives for beginners). After the trial, a top photo against a printed protractor ring gives the turn between the two marks. A caliper on the band's top says which turn it is on. No force is measured. |
| Construct validity: "awards full credit to an overtightened band" | An over-tight band now scores **0.5**, not 1.0. Red team `overtight` turned the band 202 degrees past contact and scored 0.5 (see *Validation*). |
| "update the simulated scoring or its documented approximation accordingly" | The simulator now has the closure's give. The rim's sealing surface is a sprung link, so a band can be turned on past contact as a real one can, by compressing the compound and flexing the lid and flange. Before, it was rigid, and fingertip-tight and cranked-down looked alike. The scorer reads the band's angle past its first-contact angle, the quantity the real trial reads from the marks. It does not read the spring or any force. `task.json` `scoring` is the text of `level()` and `Trial.step()`, and `fidelity` now describes the give and its estimated stiffness. |
| "specify how to check the disc's final centring and flatness when its edge is covered by the band" | The check is made through the band's 58 mm opening, with the band left on. A paper centre target (concentric rings 1 mm apart) is stuck centred on the lid at preparation. The top photo gives the lid's offset from the band, from the gaps between the opening's edge and the target's outer ring, and the band's offset from the jar, from the gaps between the skirt and the shoulder; together they give the lid's offset from the jar's axis. Flatness comes from the caliper's depth rod onto the lid's face through the opening at three points. Nothing is unscrewed before it is read. |

The scene layout, objects and instruction are unchanged. The only scene change is inside the jar: the sprung sealing surface, which the
band reaches only once it is threaded on. The Dream-1 run never lifted the band off the counter, so its score (0.0) stands.
